newsitem.title: USA: Growers say U.S. spring wheat prices need to rise.
newsitem.headline: Growers say U.S. spring wheat prices need to rise.

text.p: Wheat growers from the northern U.S. grain belt warned this week that if wheat prices remain unattractive, other crops will edge out spring wheat when farmers decide what to plant later this year.

Several growers attending the annual conference of the National Association of Wheat Growers said that if wheat prices do not rise farmers may opt to plant other crops, especially canola and field peas.

"The long and short of it is that everything aside, if new crop bids remain as they are now, spring wheat acreage will be down substantially," said Lowell Berntson, a North Dakota spring wheat grower.

"There's a lot of time between now and when we plant the crop in April and May, and people's intentions will change several times. But right now the price isn't in spring wheat," said Tim Dufault, president of the Minnesota Association of Wheat Growers.
Asked at what price wheat became an attractive planting option, growers generally cited a bid of $4 per bushel.

The wheat industry is still coming to terms with the recently disclosed shortfall in winter wheat sowings. Last Friday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said that winter wheat plantings totalled a 19-year low of 48.2 million acres, compared to average trade estimates of 51 million acres.
In 1996, U.S. growers planted 20.0 million acres to spring wheat, versus 17.0 million in 1995 and 18.3 million in 1994.

Analysts said the low winter wheat plantings data reflected landmark 1996 U.S. farm legislation, known as "Freedom to Farm," which lifted most federal controls on crop seeding in exchange for a cap on annual subsidy spending.
"If the new crop bid to me was $4, I'd consider planting (spring wheat). But that would also depend on where the other crops were bid at," Dufault said.
Wheat bids in North Dakota vary, although current cash bids for old crop spring wheat in the Red River Valley spring wheat heartland were around $3.80 per bushel, Dufault said.
Minneapolis Grain Exchange Sept 1997 spring wheat futures on Thursday closed at $3.56-1/2.
"There's some interchange with corn and soybeans, but more of a competing crop is canola, barley, sunflower, and field peas," Berntson said, citing farmers' planting options.
Growers said their planting decisions were based now more than ever on market prices.

"We respond to prices, especially with the new Farm Bill, which decouples us from payments per acre. Before you had to plant some of a commodity to get the payment for that commodity. But now we're going to raise what we're going to make money doing. That's the beauty of the system," Berntson said.
Some growers said there were other elements that could cause farmers to shift away from spring wheat.

Dufault explained that in the Red River Valley, the large wheat-growing area on the North Dakota-Minnesota border, growers were worried about scab, a fungal disease that has been a problem there for four years.
Scab can produce vomitoxin, a potentially toxic substance that devalues wheat.
Dufault also said infestations by the orange wheat blossom midge have been "scaring people away" from planting wheat.
